utterances.text: Well, I'm going to stop you there for a moment, sir. First of all, you said that you ran into a woman at the Kula school. Can you indicate where that is located in relation to Pilica town.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: May I explain. Not at the school itself, but some 50 metres away from the school on the road leading to the school near a shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the name of the school?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Vuk Karadzic, but we referred to it locally as the Kula school. Its real name was the Vuk Karadzic primary school in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The neighbour of Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And do you remember your conversation with this woman? What did she say to you? What did she ask you?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: She said: Pero, do you know what's going to happen here? I said: I don't know. What's the problem? And she said: I've been told by some soldiers from the unit, from the battalion, that we should watch out for our houses, and if possible, to move the children out of houses near the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did she say why she was told that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: She was told that probably prisoners would be brought there and that it would not be desirable for children to look at that, because the children would gather around the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And you then said you met a member of the army, is that correct, after speaking with this woman?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you indicate first of all where -- approximately where you saw this member of the army?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the road near the school. I met him on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell the Judges what his name was.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Peric.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And do you know what unit he belonged to or which brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: A battalion of the Zvornik Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But the interpreters did not hear the name of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, can you, please, repeat the name of the battalion because the interpreters did not hear it and they need to interpret everything you said.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The infantry battalion of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you met him in front of the school or thereabouts on the road, can you describe the conversation that you had with them.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I asked him: Slavko, what's going on? What's this tension all about? And he just said that he had received some sort of telegram, that it had arrived in the battalion command, that premises should be made ready to receive prisoners, that premises should be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did he say anything else? I'm sorry, sir, did you answer that question, because I didn't hear an interpretation?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did he tell you which premises should be prepared?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably as we met near the school, I imagined it was the school premises. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is there any reason that you understood that, aside from meeting in front of the school?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Because there were no other premises in the area except for private homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did Slavko Peric tell you why they were bringing prisoners into Pilica?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me why, but I asked him who had signed this information and he said he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate that I am about to go into another area, and I see that we are about 1 or 2 minutes from the break. Subject to Your Honour, we can take the break now or I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break and we will resume at 12.30

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, before the break you were telling us about a conversation that you had with Slavko Peric. Can you indicate what you did after having this conversation.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: After that conversation, I went to the office of the local commune office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Where is that office located?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: That office is close to the main road to the Bijeljina/Zvornik main road in a settled area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you indicate if there's -- the name of the place where the office is located?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is Pilica, and it belongs to a bigger settled area called Dom. We locals call this area with several buildings Dom. And in one of those rooms, there was this office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So your office was, in fact, located inside one of the buildings which made up the Pilica Dom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So why did you go to the office in the Dom? Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I went there to check with the staff about the harvest and see about this guy who was omitted from the list and also had some other things to do. I wanted to check information about some other locals who were either to be mobilised or not, depending on whether they were engaged in some things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how were you checking this information? How were you going to go about checking information in relation to the harvest?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was going to telephone the municipal staff. The harvest started a few days before that. This man was omitted from the list for the harvest, so I wanted to put his name on the list subsequently so he would be considered for that work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you at that point telephone the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that moment from Pilica, I couldn't get the municipality. The phone lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So when you discovered that the phone lines were down, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I left the building, and I happened to meet some of the locals. We discussed the situation. I told them what I had seen around the school, and we discussed the case of this man in question. And then they -- they told me that I should check with what was going on around the school was the truth. Then I told them that the telephone lines were down, and then I told them we should go to a different place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you repeat the name of the place where the man told you wanted -- you should go to so that the interpreter can hear the place.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Cepak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you decide to go to Cepak?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Not Cepak but Sepak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for correcting me. Why did you decide to go there?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I knew people there, so I could go to their house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: For what purpose? What was your intention to go to their house?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The intention was to get hold of a telephone, to call, to check with the brigade whether what we had seen around the school was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did you go to Sepak? You have to speak up a little bit, sir, so that the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So where did you go precisely when you went to Sepak?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: We went to Mr. Jovo Ivanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I found his relative there, this man was working around the house, and in the house we were talking. I told him I needed to call the brigade to check some things, that I needed the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And did you use the telephone?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He gave me the telephone, and I called from his courtyard, from in front of the house I called the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Which brigade was that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And who answered the telephone?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The person who was a switchboard operator, and he put me through to the office of the duty operations officer, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And who did you speak to at the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you speak about? What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The conversation was short. I asked him what was going on in Pilica, whether it was true that the prisoners were coming. He told me that this was not any of my concern and that I should mind my own business.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did he say anything else in relation to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did he tell you what type of prisoners they were?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. How did you know that you were speaking to Dragan Jokic when you were on the phone?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, I worked with Dragan Jokic. His engineering unit built some roads in my local commune; that's when I met him, and he introduced himself to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, when you say he introduced himself to you, what are you referring to? When was that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is Dragan Jokic, when I introduced myself, he recognised me. So we introduced ourselves to each other, so we would avoid problems, so we knew who we were talking to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And just for clarity's sake, you're referring to the telephone conversation, he introduced himself to you in the telephone conversation. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And you've indicated, sir, that you used to work with Dragan Jokic in 1992 or in 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His engineering unit worked in the territory of my local commune. They built several kilometres of road in late 1992 and beginning of 1993. And even in 1994, I believe that they worked in Pilica. They built some embankments and repaired some roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Do you see Dragan Jokic in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is on my left side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, can you briefly describe what he's wearing.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: A black suit, a light shirt, and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, I believe the witness has identified the accused, Mr. Jokic. Now, sir, can you describe your relationship with Dragan Jokic when you were working with him on the road during those years that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Jokic and I had a very good relationship, and I have a pleasant memory of him from that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you had the conversation with Dragan Jokic on the telephone where he told you these are prisoners and it's not your concern, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I returned to Pilica, together with some of my fellow villagers who had brought me from Pilica. And we were not clear of what was going to happen. We were all thinking of how we could do something to prevent things from happening. And then it was our decision that there was nothing for us to do in order to prevent the course of things. This was just a conversation that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Pilica, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Pilica, first I took somebody home and then I did some chores around the house. I tended to my cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you at any point in time see prisoners in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Having done my chores, I left my house and went towards the local commune office in order to prepare some harvest reports and to write a written -- an application for the commission for this man. As I was passing by the Kula school, I noticed vehicles parked around the school on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you -- first of all, can you describe the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Those were buses, passenger buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And what did they contain, those buses?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I noticed people as I was passing by those buses on my left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Approximately how many buses did you see?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but I suppose that there were about 20 of those buses there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And can you describe the buses.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were blue and some of them are of other colours. Srebrenica Prevoz, Drina Prevoz, I believe I saw those buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you describe the people you saw on the buses?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I saw soldiers providing security for the buses and I saw people, but only those people that you could see from the road. I saw their faces, not all of them. I was walking past those buses. I was on foot, so I could just see some of their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. The ones that you did see, sir, were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: 95 per cent of them were men, according to my estimate. I don't remember having seen women at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And the soldiers that were providing security, sir, where were they located? Were they inside or outside the buses?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Some of them were standing in front of the buses; some of them were standing on the buses, around the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Do you know where the prisoners came from?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know their identity, but I assumed that they came from Srebrenica, that is, if those were prisoners from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: What made you assume that? Why did you -- what made you think that they came from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if they were captured in Srebrenica, then I suppose that they were escorted to this place. That's what I was thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you saw the men on the buses in front of the Pilica school in Kula, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was in the local commune office tending to my regular business, and then I think I went to the municipality of Zvornik to have a word with the commission for harvest. And I had things to do in the municipality, so that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell, sir, how far away is the -- or what's the distance between the local commune office, which you've told us is in the Pilica Dom, from the Pilica school in Kula?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Less than 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after -- you indicated, sir, that the rest of the day you spent attending to business in the office. What did you do the next morning?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I went to Zvornik to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And did you see buses on that day?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see buses on that day, because I took a different road from my house to Pilica and then continued towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you pass by the school on that day?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, when you and I met the other day with the investigator, you gave us some information in relation to the chronology of the events that took place. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And although I have the English version here, I'm going to read out to you a passage from the information that you provided us to assist you in refreshing your memory on this point. Okay. If you can just listen to what I'm about to read. "Mr. Petrovic returned to his house and remained there until the next day," which is what you just told us. "The following day, Mr. Petrovic went to Zvornik to attend to community matters. Whilst driving past the school, he noticed the buses were still parked there. Some prisoners were in the school, and some were still on the buses. The prisoners were still being guarded. He stopped at the school and remained there for about 30 minutes. He could hear voices echoing in the school corridors and saw the prisoners on the buses were dressed in civilian clothing." Do you recall telling us that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When we were talking about the time when I went to Sepak, maybe you didn't understand me tell. I told you that on my return from Sepak, I went home, did some chores, and on that same day I went to the local commune office to tend to some of my business matters. On this day when I returned from Sepak, I went home, and then I returned again. And on that same day, I spent some 30 minutes there. So what you read was about that. On the following day, I took a different road to Pilica and then continued towards Zvornik. Which means that what you have now read, that is okay. I said that, but that was on the previous day, on the 11th or the 12th, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, sir. I appreciate that. Now, I'm going to show you a photograph and ask you what it depicts, and it's Exhibit 17.2. And I believe we may have it on Sanction -- oh, we don't. If we can just have that placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is the primary school in Pilica; the name of the school is Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And where were the buses parked when you saw them on that day?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In front of the building, the part that you see here, you can't park the buses, but they were behind this other part that you can't see in this photo. This view here is in front of the school, the school courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, you've just told us that you were present for about 30 minutes and you saw men in the buses. Can you indicate what -- how they were dressed, how the prisoners were dressed.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Those men were mostly sitting -- are we talking about the prisoners or the guards providing security?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: We're first talking about the prisoners now.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Those men were sitting on the buses. I saw their upper bodies, what you could see from the road, through the windows of those buses. I noticed that their clothes were not tidy. Some of them wore civilian clothes; some were in military uniforms. I did not have any explanation for that. However, in any case, their clothes were dirty. It was hot. Some of them were wearing only vests or tee-shirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And what about the guards? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The guards were in military uniforms, different military uniforms. Their uniforms were all different. They didn't all wear one and the same type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next day you indicated that you, you went back to Zvornik. Can you explain why you went to Zvornik the next day.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I went there to tend to the matters about the harvest, some written reports about this man who was to be put on the harvest list in order to be placed under work obligation instead of being mobilised. We needed him for the harvest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So after dealing with the issue of the gentleman who wanted to be placed on a work obligation, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I returned home, having done that. I returned to Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see anything on your way home?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Somewhere around Kiseljacki Put I noticed a column of some buses, some five or six of them with people sitting on the buses. And at that moment, I assumed that they were being taken from the school towards Zvornik; that was my assumption at the time. And my assumption was that they were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Turning then to Exhibit 667, which is a map, I'm going to ask you to point out exactly where you saw these buses returning from the direction of Pilica towards the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the road to Kiseljacki. And here in this part between Kozluk and Padine, the road forks off towards Kiseljacki. So thereabouts, in the vicinity of that place, around this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And can you point to Rocevic for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the place, please, I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Could you point to Rocevic on the map for us, please. I think you can move the map a bit lower.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here's Rocevic. Here, in this part here, this is Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So for the record you're pointing to the upper area of the map and it says Rocevic. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, sir. Now, when you returned to Pilica on that day, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I went back to my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that was in the Pilica Dom?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you speak to anybody there?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: As I was passing by, I did have a word with some of my fellow villagers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And aside from speaking to a fellow villager, did you speak to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is there anyone there that you met up with, sir, that you spoke to on that day in the Pilica Dom area? Is there anyone who made a request of you?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: An hour, or two hours after my arrival at the office, somebody came from the military and asked me for a key for the big community hall in the Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did you give them a key?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have the key. Somebody, an employee of Agroprom had the key.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did he say why he needed the key?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: He just told me to unlock the gym so that he could put the prisoners in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to now show you a photograph, Exhibit 19.3, if we could have the assistance of Madam Usher, please. Thank you. And I'm going to ask you, sir, if you recognise this photograph. What does this depict?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the buildings of the Dom. In one part is the local office, and behind the back is the Dom hall or gym.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Do we -- so the Dom/gym which the soldier wanted the key for is depicted -- would be in the back of this building. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can show you the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Could you point to that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's the door that leads into the hall or the gym that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, after you spoke to this soldier about the keys, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: He asked me for a hammer or a wrench so that he could open the door on his own. I said I didn't have anything like that, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And after he left, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I finished some business of mine, then I looked out of the window and saw buses full of men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And after you saw that, did you remain in your office or did you leave your office?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: After a short time, I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Turning then to Exhibit Number 666, I'm going to ask that that be placed on the overhead projector and ask you what that depicts. Now, sir, when you and I met in the office yesterday, you actually drew this diagram. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you first of all tell us what you entitled it. What's the title, on top?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In front of the building here is the area of the Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And looking then at the upper-most block, which appears to be a block of buildings, can you explain what that refers to? You have some words written there.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says warehouse of the Agroprom company, if it's this part here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, this whole area, the circular area containing the buildings is what you explained to us is the Dom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the surrounding area, we call it all Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you point out your office for us. Where is your office located?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It is marked with the words -- what words there in Serbian? How is it marked?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Local office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, behind that local office, sir, there is another building. Can you explain to us what that building represents.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the hall, the youth hall we used to call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And this youth hall which you pointed out to us, what was happening in there? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In what period?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: On that same day, sir --

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: What function?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You just told us, sir, you looked out your window and saw buses full of men. Did you see where the men were being taken at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have to use this exhibit again. The buses were parked here on this part of the road, the Dom Kosa road. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Which you have marked there. Yes, go ahead, please. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: And I noticed as I was leaving the office that the men were disembarking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Were you able to see in which direction they were going?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Towards the entrance to the hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And, sir, you've indicated that you saw this as you were leaving. Where were you going?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was going in front of the Zvornik/Bijeljina main road, and there was a restaurant opposite. I was walking towards the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And what did you do at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I probably wanted to have a cup of coffee or a glass of juice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you go anywhere else aside from the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the restaurant for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do after you stayed in the restaurant? Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the restaurant, I asked the owner -- we were talking about the prisoners. I asked him to buy a certain amount of bread for the prisoners. And from that restaurant, I went to another restaurant about 100 metres away and I found the owner of that restaurant and asked him to buy some bread, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you ask to have bread bought for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I felt compassion, and I thought that it would be more normal if they got food.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know whether the bread was delivered to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: After those two promised to get bread, I returned to my office. They came to the office door, they brought bread in bags, and I called one of the guards there and asked him to distribute the bread to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how did the guard respond when you asked him to do this?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe he didn't even know who I was because I was in civilian clothes. He looked at me. I didn't even see how he responded. I got into the car and went -- no, they got in the car and went back to the restaurant, and I walked on foot after them. It was some 70 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But you've just told us that you gave the soldiers some bread. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The soldier who was closest to me unloaded the bread from the cars. He was looking more at the people who had brought the bread than at me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So my question is: Did he say anything when he took the bread?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear him say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he did, because I'm sure I would remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: After delivering the bread to the prisoners, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: A guard took charge of the bread and went off to distribute it, and I went to the restaurant with the restaurant owners to have coffee with them and to chat to them. The people who had brought the bread, that is, they went off by car and I set out on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did you go home later on that evening?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that corner here, on the main road, a car stopped as I was about to cross the street to the restaurant and a policeman got out. He said hello to me; he probably knew me, but right now I can't remember him, who he was. He said: Pero, you look tired. Up to that moment, I hadn't really thought about this. And he asked me to go home. And I replied I didn't know how I would pass through that part of the road that went by the school. He asked me: Is there another route you can take? And I said: Yes. A car came by and he stopped the driver and asked him to give me a lift home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And did you go home?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: This was just before nightfall. I think it was a Saturday, and all that night and the next day and the next night -- I'm 50 per cent sure it was a Saturday. So a night, a day, another night, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you leave your house next, which day?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Dom or my home?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your home. You said you went there and you slept and you stayed home for a couple of days. Then did you -- when was the next time you left your home?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I went home on Saturday, it means I went back on Monday morning. I was -- let me explain. I was at home one evening, one day, another evening, another day, and then in the morning I went to the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when -- you say you went to the office. In the morning, you returned to the area of the Pilica Dom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And then turning back then to your diagram, sir, which I believe is still on the overhead projector, can you explain to us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Going towards the entrance to my office, in this area here, this is where the entrance is, I saw a truck marked here and soldiers standing around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record, you pointed out a truck parked right in front of the youth hall. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you said there were soldiers standing around it?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were loading corpses of people who had been killed, as far as I was able to discern from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Do you recall how many people were loading the corpses?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: From where I was standing, I couldn't come to any conclusion, but probably three, four, or five. I couldn't see all of them. I saw between two and five.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: They had tee-shirts, sports tee-shirts, and some sort of olive gray trousers that seemed to belong to a uniform. That's what I was able to observe. The clothes were uniform; they were the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the truck that you saw, sir, was that a military truck or a civilian truck, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't coloured in a way that would look like an army truck. I don't know whether it was the military or a civilian who was in charge of it. Is that what you asked me?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to describe the truck, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with types of vehicles. It was just a truck with a trailer. I don't know what the difference is. It was just a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know where the bodies were buried ultimately?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: A few days later, I heard the local people saying that they were buried on the Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever report this to the authorities, what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't report it, because I didn't know to whom I should report or what. I thought that the municipal and military authorities knew about what had happened in Pilica. I simply didn't know who I was supposed to report it to, officially I mean. I probably told people about it, people from the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Are you aware of any investigation into these events, sir, by the Bosnian Serb government?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I never heard anything about this, nor did I speak about it to anyone, apart from you from the Tribunal. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, I understand that when you and I met yesterday, you had a chance to review your statement. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I understand that you made some notations and some changes to a couple of parts in your statement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And perhaps I can just show you a copy of your statement to help you refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you explain the nature of the changes that you made.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: When I was interviewed by your investigator, I gave the chronology of events in a certain order. And when I signed this document, I realised that what it says here represents the essence of these events; however, yesterday I noticed that the order of sentences and paragraphs and the sequence of events is not right. And yesterday, I made an observation. I wrote this in front of you so that it would be easier for me to tell the events in their proper chronological sequence, which is why, for example, here I noted down -- may I read?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: For example, in the first paragraph it says: "On the 12th of June," and I remembered that it was not June, but July. It's probably a mistake. It says: "People from Srebrenica were brought to Pilica." And then it goes on to say: "On that day about 20 buses full of Muslim men were brought to Pilica. I personally counted them." Yesterday I noted down that even if I stated that I had counted them personally, then we couldn't say approximately. And then there was a big problem as to how the Court would understand this. I counted them personally. I don't know what the translator or the person compiling this document, what they meant by this. Then it says here -- it should say: "In front of the shop. I saw soldiers arriving. A woman," that's what I said just a little while ago, "was standing in front of me and she said: Pero, do you know what's happening? I told her I didn't know." This part here happened before the prisoners arrived. Then in the second paragraph, the military staff sent some soldiers. I know that I never used the expression "military staff." It should say here the "battalion command" to tell people. I think it should say "the local villages to remove people from the surrounding houses." I found a man from the headquarters. I think it would be better to say: "I came across or ran into a man from the headquarters. His name was Slavko Peric and I asked him what was the problem. He said that he had received from Standard headquarters." I never used this expression. I always used the words "brigade command." And that he had received a telegram from them that some prisoners would arrive there. This also happened, this incident, before the arrival of the prisoners. And then the third paragraph, I went to Sepak, this is okay, but this also happened before the arrival of the prisoners. The fourth paragraph, first sentence, I just saw the dead bodies when they loaded them. This should be the seventh sentence of this paragraph. It should follow after sentence number six. The soldiers from Srebrenica were the ones who brought the detainees to Pilica. I just said that the detainees were brought by soldiers. I mentioned the security men whom I assume loaded the prisoners. I do not know which soldiers belong to which unit. None of them introduced themselves to me, and then I never asked anyone where they came from. And I never asked anyone where they came from. You could say I had no contact with the soldiers or the security guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, I did not see any digging machine going in that direction, because it had been done during the night. I did not see any digging machine going in that direction. As I gave this statement 12 months ago, I assume that the investigator of The Hague Tribunal asked me whether I had seen any machines going in the direction of Branjevo. I didn't see any digging machine going in that direction. This was probably a response to a question. And then because it had been done during the night. There may be a mistake in the translation here. I may have said it's possible that this was done, because the way it stands now -- because it looks as if I'm claiming that this was done during the night. I can't say that because I didn't see it. Nobody came and asked me for my assistance; this was probably a response to a question as to whether anyone from the Army of Republika Srpska had come to me in the local commune to ask for assistance. And I replied to this question that nobody came and asked me for any assistance. And then it says: "I assume that the VRS soldiers did it and that they didn't need assistance from the local population." Probably I was asked who this -- who could have done this. We didn't see anything, it says. This was a question put to me. And the answer should be: "I didn't see anything, as Branjevo is not on the main road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But I think that this is a serious digression of the proceedings here. This is supposed to be question, answer form. If the Prosecution wants to have him change his statement, can we have it in the form of their, you know, proofing notes that they are so accustomed to providing for us the day of the witness's testimony. So perhaps we should break today, let them get their statements together, and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I entirely agree with you as for the reasons, but as for the approach, we'll see the response from the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, we were just getting to the end. I asked the witness to describe the nature of the changes, and he did. It was rather lengthy, I agree, but I didn't want to interrupt the witness. And he was responding to that question that I was asking him. I can certainly move on. I mean the Defence has been provided with a copy of the changes that the witness had made himself on the statement so that they do have that. Unfortunately, of course, due to the time, those changes -- that had not yet been translated. We have not had an opportunity to make a translation of his notes. And part of what I was trying achieve today is also to deal with that issue, given that it had not as of yet been translated, as we only received this information yesterday so that there was not sufficient time to translate it. I will move on. I am close to the end of my examination. In fact, I believe I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on. And I hope in the future you could give the proper lead to this witness as for the evidence of the privileged statement. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but if I understand Ms. Issa, she wants to complete her examination-in-chief with another question, so I believe that it would be fair of us to let the witness complete his list of objections. Because we are coming to a sentence which may be a topic of the cross-examination. So we want to do that. So when he explained the sentence: A digging machine came and took them away, in the handwritten corrections, there is a correction of this mistake, so why don't we bring this to an end and then I would have one passage less to tackle in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you still have the opportunity to ask about this question in your cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may be heard for one second. One, I would concur with Mr. Stojanovic, only because this is an occasion where a statement was taken from a witness but it wasn't tape recorded, it would appear. And so we have a summary of what this gentleman had told an investigator, and then it appears that just only yesterday he had an opportunity to review what it is that he allegedly told the investigators when he was questioned. That's part of the problem. And I understand that the gentleman now has been given an opportunity to read a translated version of what he allegedly had told the investigators from the OTP and has some grave reservation as to what exactly he said, at least on some points. So I would agree that at least since he's already begun outlining the disagreements with his statement or he's trying to provide some clarification, that it might be useful to allow him to finish that at this point in time so we have at least a clear record on how he feels about the statement that he allegedly has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, for the specific issue about that digging machine, Ms. Issa, you may ask some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I will continue on with that. I just want to indicate, just so that it's clear, Your Honour, that the investigator who initially took the statement was not a member of our team and may not have the whole story. In other words, was not aware of the events as they took place, and that may explain as to the potential problems that may have arisen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were indicating in that very last paragraph, you were talking about -- the last thing I believe you corrected was the word "I" instead of we. Where it says: "I could not see anything because Branjevo was not along the main road." There are a couple more sentences after that. Is there anything there that you see which you think requires a change?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to thank you all for giving me this opportunity. It is correct that this statement was read to me, but it was after seven or eight hours of me being interviewed. I understood it as the essence being correct, however the sequence and -- the sequence of sentences and words is something that I would like to correct. In the last passage we left it off as we didn't see; however, this was my interview. So it should read: "I didn't see." Since Branjevo is not on the main road, so one couldn't see exactly what was going on. If they had informed me, then we have to insert here: "I would have known." So what I was saying to the investigator is if I had been informed, I would have known. Later on I was informed that a digging machine came and took them away. I'm not happy with this passage and this sentence, because in this sentence it says: "Later on I heard that bodies were taken away. I don't know where." So I can't say a digging machine came and took the bodies away. I could not say that at the time. Later on I heard that a digging machine had come and took the bodies away, but as far as I know a digging machine cannot take bodies away. A digging machine does precisely that, digs and excavates. It cannot carry bodies anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much, sir, for informing us of all of that.

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I just want to go back to one issue that we discussed earlier, sir, and that's in relation to your conversation with Dragan Jokic at the start before the prisoners -- before you saw the prisoners at Pilica. Now, do you recall specifically about the way in which the prisoners were referred to by Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Jokic and I knew each other. The last time I spoke to him, Jokic told me - I didn't feel anything - he just told me: This is not your concern. Go home and tend to your own business.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sir, I'm going to ask you - and I believe you have a copy of your statement in front of you - to look at the statement to assist you in refreshing your memory. And I would also refer to the proofing notes --

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's all right. I'll direct you, sir, to I believe somewhere around paragraph 3. Does reading that passage assist you --

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you a question, sir. Does that passage assist you in refreshing your memory as to more specifically what Dragan Jokic said to you in relation to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to quote Dragan Jokic, but when it says here: These are prisoners of war, go home. This is the essence of it. That's what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, sir, what you indicated in the proofing session when you and I met the other day? For the sake of completeness, perhaps I'll read it and ask you if it assists you in refreshing your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I'm referring to page 2 at about line 7 from the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It says: "Mr. Jokic told Mr. Petrovic over the telephone that the prisoners he spoke of were military prisoners and it was not the concern of Petrovic and that there were people taking care of this." Does that assist you in refreshing your memory as to who he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose he was referring to the military, because this was information from the brigade, from an officer. So I suppose he was referring to them, and that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: PERO PETROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that for a fact. He simply told me that I should stay out of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have only one minute left, so we have to stop now. Witness, as I did to other witnesses in this case, that since you are in The Hague, you are under the oath, so do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, after the witness is gone, I can give you the briefest of updates where we are for witnesses for the rest of the week or I can do that tomorrow. We had spoken with counsel and they would appreciate something on the record there also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We're on our schedule, if people have it. We will be able to start with -- and could we go into private session so I can say the name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
